title: The Battle of Fort Dearborn
premise: April to August 1812 in twelve stops, from the killings at Lee's Place to the march down the beach, the surrender, and the houses where the Kinzies and Mrs. Helm hid.

opening.text: JAUNT: THE BATTLE OF FORT DEARBORN. 6 April to 16 August 1812, twelve stops in date order: a farm three miles up the South Branch, the fort and the houses round it, the river mouth, a mile and a half of beach, and the Kinzie house on the north bank. Fly is set: the stops are far apart. Every date and quotation is from the record, and where the record argues with itself the stop says so: Captain Heald's own report and journal, General Hull's order, the Kinzie family's Wau-Bun, and Quaife's history of 1913, which doubts some of Wau-Bun's best scenes. Every account was written by the garrison's side or by settler historians. No one is drawn; the places are.

stops.text: 6 April 1812, a little before sunset. Eleven men walked into this cabin on the South Branch, 'about three miles from the garrison', and killed Liberty White and a Canadian hand. Heald supposed them Winnebagoes. A discharged soldier and Lee's son slipped over to the haystacks on this bank, as if to fodder the cattle, and ran for the fort.

That evening the two runners shouted across the river to the Burns house to get out. Ensign Ronan took five or six soldiers upriver in a scow and 'took the mother, with her infant of scarcely a day old, upon her bed to the boat'. The fort fired a cannon to call in a fishing party. Heald enrolled fifteen militia.

9 August. A runner, Winnemac, brought General Hull's order from Detroit: 'It is with regret I order the Evacuation of your Post owing to the want of Provisions'. The arms were to be destroyed; the factory's goods could be given away. Wau-Bun says the officers begged Heald to stay and fortify. He chose to obey.

12 August by Wau-Bun, the 13th by Quaife. The Potawatomi of the villages around had come in 'from all quarters', as Heald wrote, and he met them in council on this open ground. His officers would not go. They manned the blockhouses above it, 'opened the port-holes, and pointed the cannon so as to command the whole assembly'.

13 or 14 August. Out of this store, the government's trading house, went everything on its shelves: 'blankets, broadcloths, calicoes, paints'. Heald gave away 'a considerable quantity of provisions which we could not take away with us' as well. Hull's order allowed the goods. The powder and the liquor were another matter.

That night muskets were broken and dropped with powder, shot and flints down a well in the sally-port. The liquor went out through the northern gate, 'the heads of the barrels knocked in, and the contents poured into the river'. The knocking gave it away. Next morning, Wau-Bun says, the river tasted of 'strong grog'.

13 or 14 August. Captain William Wells rode in from Fort Wayne with a Miami escort to bring out his niece, Rebekah Heald, and her husband, but 'all too late'. That evening Black Partridge, a Potawatomi leader, gave back his peace medal: 'I will not wear a token of peace while I am compelled to act as an enemy.'

15 August, nine in the morning. The column came down the river to its mouth here and turned south along the beach: Wells ahead, the soldiers, the wagons of children, the twelve militia. Wau-Bun says the band struck up the Dead March and Wells had 'blackened his face'. Mrs. Kinzie's boat, warned, waited at this mouth.

'We had proceeded about a mile and a half,' Heald wrote, 'when it was discovered that the Indians were prepared to attack us from behind the bank.' About here, by his measure. The soldiers charged up it. Behind them the wagons were overrun; the militia died to a man, and with them Cicely, an enslaved servant, and her baby son.

Heald pulled his last men back to 'a small elevation in the open prarie'. The Potawatomi leader Black Bird came out, shook hands and asked him to surrender, 'promising to spare the lives of all the prisoners'. Heald counted 52 dead, twelve of them children. Later Chicago remembered two cottonwoods near here as the place.

15 and 16 August. Here the Kinzies held out. Mrs. Heald was carried in wounded, and Kinzie cut a ball from her arm 'with his penknife'. Next day a war party with blackened faces sat down silent in the parlor. Billy Caldwell walked in 'with a calm step', greeted them as friends, and they left with cotton for their dead.

16 August. Dressed as a Frenchwoman of the country, Margaret Helm was hidden in this house under the edge of a feather bed, face to the wall, while Mrs. Bisson sat on the bed sewing. 'I can but die,' Mrs. Helm begged; 'let them put an end to my misery at once.' The searchers looked round the room and left.

legs.note: Far: about three miles down the river to the fort. Fly, or go Instantly.
legs.story: Down the bank in the dusk the soldier and the boy ran for the fort, calling across the water as they went.
Four months on. War with Britain was declared in June; the news came to the fort in August.
Out of the gate to the open ground west of the stockade.
West past the agency house to the factory.
Round to the river side of the fort, where the covered way runs down to the water.
Back round to the main gate on the south side.
Down the river's west bank, the way the column marched.

legs.note: Far: a mile down the beach. Fly, or go Instantly.
legs.story: South with 'the lake on our left, and a high sand bank on our right'.
Inland and south along the shore, toward the later Eighteenth Street.

legs.note: Far: two miles back north, across the river. Fly, or go Instantly.
legs.story: The prisoners were taken back toward the fort; the Kinzies were returned to their own house.
A few steps west along the bank to Ouilmette's.

endings.text: The next morning, 16 August, the fort was set on fire. Only the brick magazine 'alone defied the fire'. On the third day the Kinzies were put into a boat for St. Joseph; the Healds, both wounded, were taken across the lake the day after the battle; the surviving soldiers, women and children were carried off until the next spring, when they were 'for the most part, carried to Detroit and ransomed'. Mrs. Lee and her baby were among them, and Mrs. Burns with the infant carried down to the fort in April. The fort stood in ashes until 1816, when the army came back and built a second one on the same ground.

keepsake.title: Captain Heald's report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812
keepsake.text: 'I embrace this opportunity to render you an account of the garrison of Chicago.' The commander's own account of the evacuation, written ten weeks after it.

evidence.text: Captain Nathan Heald, writing from Chicago on 15 April 1812: 'On the 6th instant, a little before sunset, a party of eleven Indians, supposed to be Winnebagoes, came to Messrs. Russell and Lee's cabin, in a field on the Portage branch of the Chicago river, about three miles from the garrison, where they murdered two men, one by the name of Liberty White, an American, and the other a Canadian Frenchman whose name I do not know.' The 1895 editors add the name [Debou] in brackets.
evidence.locator: p. 43, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 6876-6890 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected: Heald's letter of 15 April 1812)

evidence.text: Wau-Bun dates the attack to the 7th and tells the escape. A discharged soldier and a boy (Lee's son, by ch. XIX) left the visitors in the cabin and walked to the two canoes tied by the bank. The soldier 'pointed to the cattle which were standing among the haystacks on the opposite bank, and made signs that they must go and fodder them'. Once across, hidden by the haystacks, 'they took to the woods' and made for the fort, hearing two shots behind them. Their story: the farm was 'occupied by a Mr. White and three persons employed by him'.
evidence.locator: ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text, the April section; ch. XIX for the boy as Lee's son

evidence.text: Wau-Bun: running down the river the two fugitives 'arrived opposite Burns's, where, as before related, they called across to advertise the family of their danger, and then hastened on to the fort.' Ensign Ronan volunteered with five or six soldiers: 'They ascended the river in a scow, and took the mother, with her infant of scarcely a day old, upon her bed to the boat'. A corporal and six men were fishing upriver, so 'the commanding officer ordered a cannon to be fired, to warn them of danger.'
evidence.locator: ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text, the April section

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'after the murders at the Lee farm, Captain Heald enrolled fifteen militiamen from the civilian population outside the fort.' Wau-Bun: the people outside the fort 'now intrenched themselves in the Agency House'; its piazzas 'were planked up, for greater security, port-holes were cut, and sentinels posted at night.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, the chapter on the first fort (Gutenberg #69274 plain text, the paragraph on the civilians around the fort); Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: General William Hull's order, Sandwich, 29 July 1812, found among the Heald papers and first printed by Quaife: 'It is with regret I order the Evacuation of your Post owing to the want of Provisions only a neglect of the Commandant' ... 'You will therefore Destroy all arms & ammunition, but the Goods of the Factory you may give to the Friendly Indians who may be desirous of Escorting you on to Fort Wayne & to the Poor & needy of your Post.'
evidence.locator: note 583, Gutenberg #69274 plain text, the evacuation chapter

evidence.text: Heald's journal: 'On the 9th of Augt, 1812, rec'd orders from Genl Wm. Hull to evacuate the Post of Chicago and proceed with my Command to Detroit.' Quaife: 'The next day the Indian runner. Winnemac, delivered to Captain Heald at Fort Dearborn his order for the evacuation.' Wau-Bun puts the runner, Winnemeg or Catfish, a Potawatomi, at the post on the 7th, bringing despatches that 'announced the declaration of war between the United States and Great Britain'. Wau-Bun: 'The order for evacuating the post was read next morning upon parade', and the officers' 'unanimous advice was, to remain where they were, and fortify themselves as strongly as possible.' Quaife defends Heald: 'Obedience to orders is the primary duty of a soldier.'
evidence.locator: Quaife Appendix III (Heald's journal) and the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'The neighboring Indians got the information as early as I did, and came in from all quarters in order to receive the goods in the factory store, which they understood were to be given them.' His warriors on the 15th were 'mostly of the Potawatamie nation' (the Potawatomi, as the name is now written). Wau-Bun puts a council on the afternoon of the 12th: 'Captain Heald alone attended on the part of the military.' His officers 'took command of the block-houses which overlooked the esplanade on which the council was held, opened the port-holes, and pointed the cannon so as to command the whole assembly.' Quaife thinks the council was 'probably' on the 13th.
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife note 589 and the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 14th, I delivered the Indians all the goods in the factory store, and a considerable quantity of provisions which we could not take away with us.' Wau-Bun, which dates it the 13th: 'the goods, consisting of blankets, broadcloths, calicoes, paints, etc., were distributed, as stipulated.'
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'The surplus arms and ammunition I thought proper to destroy, fearing they would make bad use of it if put in their possession. I also destroyed all the liquor on hand after they began to collect.' Wau-Bun: 'the ammunition and liquor were carried, part into the sally-port, and thrown into a well which had been dug there to supply the garrison with water in case of emergency; the remainder was transported as secretly as possible through the northern gate, the heads of the barrels knocked in, and the contents poured into the river.' The muskets 'were broken up and thrown into the well'. The noise betrayed it, and 'the taste of the water the next morning was, as one expressed it, "strong grog."'
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 13th, Captain Wells, of Fort Wayne, arrived with about 30 Miamies, for the purpose of escorting us in, by the request of General Hull.' Wau-Bun has him arrive on the 14th 'with fifteen friendly Miamis' to save 'his relative, Captain Heald', and says he came 'all too late': the ammunition was already destroyed. Quaife: Heald's wife Rebekah was 'the niece of Captain Wells'.
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Wau-Bun: on the evening after the second council 'Black Partridge, a conspicuous chief, entered the quarters of the commanding officer' and gave back his medal: 'I will not wear a token of peace while I am compelled to act as an enemy.' Quaife: Black Partridge was 'a Pottawatomie chief from the Illinois River' (a Potawatomi leader); of the two contemporary versions, Lieutenant Helm's and Sergeant Griffith's through McAfee, both record his warning and 'Helm alone mentions the surrender of the medal.'
evidence.locator: ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text; Quaife, the evacuation chapter and note 591

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 15th, at 9 o'clock in the morning, we commenced our march: a part of the Miamies were detached in front, and the remainder in our rear, as guards, under the direction of Captain Wells. The situation of the country rendered it necessary for us to take the beach, with the lake on our left, and a high sand bank on our right, at about 100 yards distance.' Wau-Bun: 'As the troops left the fort, the band struck up the Dead March', and Wells 'had blackened his face before leaving the garrison, in token of his impending fate.' Mrs. Kinzie's boat 'had scarcely reached the mouth of the river, which, it will be recollected, was here half a mile below the fort, when another messenger from To-pee-nee-bee arrived to detain them where they were.' Quaife lists the order: Wells and part of the Miamis, the garrison, the women and children, the twelve Chicago militia.
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the battle chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XIX, Narrative of the Massacre, Continued, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'We had proceeded about a mile and a half, when it was discovered that the Indians were prepared to attack us from behind the bank. I immediately marched up with the company to the top of the bank, when the action commenced; after firing one round, we charged, and the Indians gave way in front and joined those on our flanks.' Quaife: 'Meanwhile a deadlier combat, which we may perhaps think of as a separate battle, was raging around the wagons in the rear.' The militia 'were cut down to a man'. Among the dead were 'Cicely, Mrs. Heald's negro serving-woman' and 'her infant son, who also perished', two of the few recorded people held in slavery at Chicago.
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the battle chapter and note 596

evidence.text: This stand is on the reconstructed 1812 beach at Heald's 'about a mile and a half', measured along the march from the fort site down the river and the shore.
evidence.reasoning: data/terrain/1812_evacuation_readings.json and the route tools/derive_evacuation_1812.py lays from it: the station 'About a mile and a half (Heald)' at local E 1318.0, N -1852.7, the middle of a band of 1.25 to 1.75 miles. The stand is 6 m inland of it. It is a reading of his distance, not a marked place, and the scene card 'Where the attack happened' says the same.

evidence.text: Heald's report: he 'took possession of a small elevation in the open prarie, out of shot of the bank or any other cover' and was met 'by one of the Potawatamie chiefs, called the Black Bird' (a Potawatomi leader), who 'requested me to surrender, promising to spare the lives of all the prisoners.' The toll he gives: 'twenty-six regulars and all the militia were killed in the action, with two women and twelve children. Ensign George Ronan and doctor Isaac V Van Voorhis of my company, with Captain Wells, of Fort Wayne, are, to my great sorrow, numbered among the dead.' The warriors numbered 'between four and five hundred', and their loss 'was about fifteen.' The report opens: 'I embrace this opportunity to render you an account of the garrison of Chicago.'
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text

evidence.text: Two cottonwoods in the later Eighteenth Street were remembered as the place of the attack, a tradition written down from the 1880s; this scene stands them where it put them, and Heald's own mile and a half falls short of them.
evidence.reasoning: The scene's card 'Where the attack happened' and data/terrain/1812_evacuation_readings.json weigh the tradition against Heald's distance; Isaac Arnold's letter of 1884 (Kirkland, Appendix K) has 'some cottonwood trees near which I was told the massacre occurred.' The camera is the scene's own anchor eighteenth_street_shore.

evidence.text: Wau-Bun: Mrs. Heald, badly wounded, was ransomed by Kinzie's clerk Chandonnai for a mule and the promise of whiskey and brought to the boat, and then to the house, where 'Mr. Kinzie then performed the operation himself, with his penknife.' 'At their own mansion the family of Mr. Kinzie were closely guarded by their Indian friends.' On the 16th 'Black Partridge, Wau-ban-see, and Kee-po-tah, with two other Indians' sat in the porch as sentinels. A party from the Wabash, who had 'blackened their faces', came into the parlor and 'seated themselves upon the floor in silence'. Then Billy Caldwell, the Sauganash, 'entered the parlor with a calm step', laid his rifle behind the door and greeted them as friends; 'thus taken by surprise', they 'said modestly that they came to beg of their friends some white cotton in which to wrap their dead before interring them.'
evidence.locator: ch. XIX, Narrative of the Massacre, Continued, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Wau-Bun: Black Partridge had Mrs. Helm put on 'the ordinary dress of a Frenchwoman of the country' and led her to Ouilmette's house. When the searchers came, the household 'raised a large feather bed and placed her under the edge of it, upon the bedstead, with her face to the wall', and Mrs. Bisson, the sister of Ouilmette's wife, 'seated herself with her sewing upon the front of the bed.' Nearly suffocating, Mrs. Helm begged to be given up: 'I can but die,' said she; 'let them put an end to my misery at once.' The searchers looked about the room 'and left the house.' Quaife (1913) warns that this part of Wau-Bun may be heightened: 'That Black Partridge saved Mrs. Helm is probably true, but that the affair possessed the romantic aspect which it has come to assume in the popular mind ... seems unlikely.' Her first name is in Kirkland (1893): 'Margaret Helm, wife of Lieutenant Helm, and step-daughter of old John Kinzie'.
evidence.locator: ch. XIX, Narrative of the Massacre, Continued, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text; Kirkland 1893, the opening chapter, footnote [A] (Gutenberg #59624 plain text, line 590); Quaife Appendix II, on Mrs. Helm's narrative

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'The next morning, they set fire to the fort and left the place, taking the prisoners with them.' Quaife: the magazine, 'a small structure made of brick', 'alone defied the fire'. Wau-Bun: 'On the third day after the battle, the family of Mr. Kinzie, with the clerks of the establishment, were put into a boat' for St. Joseph. The prisoners, Wau-Bun says, were dispersed among the villages 'until the following spring, when they were, for the most part, carried to Detroit and ransomed'; Mrs. Lee and her infant were taken to Black Partridge's village on the Au Sable, and Mrs. Burns 'with her infant, became the prisoner of a chief'. Heald's journal: 'On the 16th, that is the day after [the] action, Mrs. Heald & myself were taken to the St. Joseph River by our new Masters.' The army came back in 1816 and began the second fort on the same site (Quaife, the chapter on the second fort). Quaife on Wau-Bun as a whole: its accounts 'all proceed, directly or indirectly from a common source', and do Heald 'grave injustice'.
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the description of the fort and the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XIX, Narrative of the Massacre, Continued, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text
